νόμον τηρεῖ· πέπαυται γάρ. πτωχὰ δὲ στοιχεῖα εἰπὼν οὐ κατηγόρησεν ὡς πονηρῶν,
ἀλλ' ὡς πλουτίζειν μὴ δυναμένων καὶ ἀρκεῖν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. 302 Gal 4,12 Μὴ
νομίσητε, φησίν, ὅτι ἄλλην τινὰ λύπην εἶχον πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐπιπλήττω·
τῆς γὰρ ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος συνεχῶς αὐτὸν μεταβάλλειν ἀναγκάζει τοῦ λόγου τὸ εἶδος,
καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐπιτιμᾶν, νῦν δὲ παρακαλεῖν, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν κατηγορεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ θρηνεῖν.
ἐνταῦθα τοίνυν διδάσκει ὡς ἅπερ γράφει, διὰ φιλοστοργίαν γράφει–οὐδὲν γάρ, φησί,
παρ' ὑμῶν ἠδίκημαι–, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν, ὅτι μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι. Gal 4,15–
18 Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς. ἢ οὕτως· τὸ τηρεῖν νόμον ἢ τὸ πίστει ζῆν;
καὶ ἐπειδὴ εἶπεν ὅτι ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἵνα τὸ τέλειον αὐτοὶ ἔχωσι
τῆς πίστεως μὴ τηροῦντες νόμον, ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἐπήγαγεν ὅτι ταῦτα
λέγω οὐ φθονῶν αὐτοῖς· ὤφελον γὰρ κἀκεῖνοι τέλειοι ἦσαν τῇ πίστει κεχρημένοι,
καὶ ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς. καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν τοιαῦτα
πράττετε ἃ καὶ ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ, ἵνα πάντες ὑμᾶς μιμῶνται, καὶ μὴ ὅταν ἔλθω
αἰδεσθέντες με τοιοῦτοι γίνεσθε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμοῦ μὴ παρόντος ἑαυτοὺς διορθοῦσθε.
Gal 4,23–24 Νῦν τῷ ὀνόματι κατεχρήσατο, οὐ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ἀλληγορίας. ἡ γὰρ
ἀλληγορία οὐ στοιχεῖ τοῖς ῥητοῖς, ἄλλα δέ τινα ἐμφαινόμενα ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὑφὴν
τῶν νοημάτων ἀκολουθίας εἰσάγει, οἷόν ἐστι τὸ φιλησάτω με ἀπὸ φιλημάτων
στόματος αὐτοῦ, τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων· ἐκεῖ γὰρ οὔτε φίλημα οὔτε θρὶξ
οὔτε κοιλία οὐδὲ μηροὶ οὐδὲ ἕτερόν τι, ἀλλ' ἄλλα δι' ἄλλων εἰσάγεται, καὶ τοῦτό
ἐστιν ἀλληγορίας εἶδος κύριον. ἐνταῦθα δὲ καὶ ἡ ἱστορία ὡμολόγηται, καὶ ὅτι τύπος
ἐστὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀποδέδεικται. ἡ οὖν δι' ἔργων προφητεία ἀλληγορία νῦν
ὠνόμασται. τῶν γὰρ προφητειῶν αἱ μέν εἰσι διὰ λόγων μόνον ὡς τὸ ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος
ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, αἱ δὲ δι' ἔργων μόνον ὡς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ,
αἱ δὲ καὶ δι' ἔργων καὶ διὰ λόγων ὡς τὸ πρὸς 303 Ἰερεμίαν ῥηθέν, τὸ λάβε περίζωμα
καινὸν καὶ περίθου· εἶτα θάψον αὐτὸ παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην, καὶ ὡς διερρύη τῷ χρόνῳ
καὶ διεβρώθη, λάβε αὐτό, φησίν, ἐκεῖθεν. ἕως γὰρ τούτου δι' ἔργων ἡ προφητεία, τὸ
δὲ ἑξῆς καὶ διὰ λόγων· ὅτι οὕτως κἀγὼ τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ περιεθέμην καὶ οὕτως
αὐτοῖς ἐβοήθησα, καὶ οὕτως αὐτοὺς εἰς Βαβυλῶνα ἀπάγω αἰχμαλώτους καὶ
σαθρωθέντας καὶ φθαρέντας ἐκεῖθεν ἀναγάγω καὶ ἀποκαθιστῶ. νῦν οὖν τὴν δι'
pass_a_gloss:
[continuing Galatians 4:8-10 from the previous section] ... keeps the law; for it has ceased. And having said "beggarly elements," he did not accuse them as evil, but as not able to make rich and to suffice for piety.
Galatians 4:12. Do not think, he says, that I had some other grief toward you and because of this I rebuke you. For the feeling of pain constantly compels him to change the form of his speech: now to censure, now to exhort, and at one time to accuse, at another to lament. Here then he teaches that what he writes, he writes through affection, for, he says, I have been wronged by you in nothing, but rather I was deemed worthy even of care, indeed of the very greatest.
Galatians 4:15-18. "What then was the blessedness?" In place of "none." Or thus: keeping the law, or living by faith? And since he had said that those men want not to emulate you, so that they themselves might have the perfection of faith while not keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added: I say these things not envying them; for would that those too were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing would hinder them from being emulated and from imitating us. And you, then, do such things as make you to be emulated, so that all may imitate you; and do not become such only when I come, out of respect for me, but even when I am not present correct yourselves.
Galatians 4:23-24. Now he used the name loosely, not with the force of allegory. For allegory does not keep in line with the things said, but brings in some other things that show through from the sequence of the thoughts according to the texture (of the text), such as "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth," the one in the Song of Songs; for there there is neither kiss nor hair nor belly nor thighs nor anything else, but some things are brought in through others, and this is the proper form of allegory. But here the history also is acknowledged, and that it is a type of what is to come has been shown. So the prophecy through deeds has now been named allegory. For of prophecies some are through words only, as "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb"; others through deeds only, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness; others both through deeds and through words, as what was said to Jeremiah: "Take a new loincloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates," and when it had rotted through time and been eaten away, "take it," he says, "from there." For up to this the prophecy is through deeds, but what follows is also through words: that so I too put on the sons of Israel, and so I helped them, and so I lead them away captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and been corrupted I will bring them up from there and I restore them. Now then the prophecy through [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … keep the law, for the law has come to an end. When he calls the elements “beggarly”, he is not accusing them of being evil. He means that they cannot make anyone rich and are not enough for true piety.

On Galatians 4:12: Do not think, he says, that I have some other grievance against you and that this is why I rebuke you. For the pain he feels keeps forcing him to change the form of his speech: now he reproves, now he encourages, at one moment he accuses, at another he laments. So here he teaches them that what he writes, he writes out of love. “You have done me no wrong,” he says; on the contrary, I was treated with care, with the greatest care of all.

On Galatians 4:15–18: “What, then, was the blessedness?” This stands for “there was none.” Or take it this way: which is blessed, keeping the law or living by faith? He had said that those men do not want to follow your example, which would give them the perfection of faith without keeping the law; they want you to follow theirs. So he went on to say: I am not saying this because I grudge them anything. I wish they too had become perfect by making use of faith; then nothing would stop them from being taken as models and from imitating us. As for you, act in a way that makes you worth following, so that everyone may imitate you. Do not become like this only when I come, out of respect for me; correct yourselves even when I am not with you.

On Galatians 4:23–24: Here he uses the word loosely, not in the proper sense of allegory. Allegory does not stay with what is actually said. It brings in something else, which shows through the sequence of thoughts woven into the text. An example is “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” in the Song of Songs (Song of Solomon 1:2). There it is not really a kiss, or hair, or a belly, or thighs, or anything of the kind; one thing is conveyed by means of another, and that is allegory properly so called. Here, though, the history is accepted as true, and it is also shown to be a type of what was to come. So what he now calls allegory is prophecy by deeds. Some prophecies are given by words alone, like “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7:14). Some are given by deeds alone, as when “Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” (John 3:14). And some are given by deeds and words together, like the command to Jeremiah: “Take a new loincloth and put it on. Then bury it by the Euphrates.” And when time had rotted it and eaten it away, “take it,” he says, “from there” (Jeremiah 13:1–7). Up to this point the prophecy is in deeds; what follows is in words as well: in this way I too wrapped the sons of Israel around me (Jeremiah 13:11), and in this way I helped them; in this way I am leading them away captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and decayed there I will bring them back and restore them. So here he has called prophecy by …

lemmas.gloss: has ceased, come to an end
beggarly, poor elements (Galatians 4:9); old English wrongly 'weak'
use loosely, use improperly (of a word)

choices.english: … keep the law, for the law has come to an end.
choices.why: Completes 'καὶ οὐ' from the end of u01-rem-early; opens with an ellipsis.
rejected: He keeps the law; for it has ceased. (old: dropped the negative that sits in the previous section)

choices.term: οὐδὲν γάρ … ἠδίκημαι–, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν, ὅτι μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι
choices.english: “You have done me no wrong,” he says; on the contrary, I was treated with care, with the greatest care of all.
choices.why: ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν … ἠξίωμαι answers 'I was not wronged' (cf. Galatians 4:13–14). The Greek mixes accusative θεραπείαν with genitive πλείστης; the sense is clear.
rejected: but also for healing, because I was most worthy (old)

choices.term: ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν … ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν
choices.english: those men do not want to follow your example … they want you to follow theirs
choices.why: Paraphrase of Galatians 4:17; the purpose clause explains what emulating the Galatians would have given them.
Technical term for catachresis: Paul's 'allegory' is not allegory in the strict sense.

choices.term: Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
choices.english: “Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” (John 3:14)
choices.why: The wording is that of John 3:14; the event is Numbers 21:9.

choices.term: οὕτως κἀγὼ τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ περιεθέμην
choices.english: in this way I too wrapped the sons of Israel around me
choices.why: Paraphrase of Jeremiah 13:11 (the girdle cleaving to the loins); the rest of the sentence (captivity, return) is Severian's own wording and carries no reference.

choices.english: So here he has called prophecy by …
choices.why: Sentence runs on into u01-rem-close ('ἔργων … ὠνόμασεν').
